opus-5.5.text:
I think what's most interesting to me is that it forces you to confront a question we've mostly been able to sidestep with frontier models: how does a model actually acquire new knowledge after pretraining? When you train on the whole internet, any given fact shows up thousands of times, in many different phrasings and contexts, so the model ends up with a robust representation almost by accident. A company's private data is the opposite. You might have one design doc that explains why a system was built a certain way, or a single Slack thread where an important decision got made. It's small, it's idiosyncratic, and a lot of it is never written down explicitly at all.

So the problem becomes: how do you get a model to really internalize a small amount of new information, not just memorize the surface tokens, but understand it well enough to reason with it, connect it to what it already knows, and use it in situations that look nothing like the original document? We know naive fine-tuning doesn't do this well. You get the reversal curse, or the model can recite the doc but can't answer a question that needs one inference step. And you often get forgetting or degradation of general capabilities.

That's why I find it such a nice research problem. It sits right at the intersection of things we don't understand well: memory, continual learning, how knowledge is stored in the weights versus retrieved in context. Retrieval and long context get you surprisingly far, but they're more like handing someone a binder than having a colleague who has been at the company for five years and just *knows* how things work. That tacit, accumulated understanding is what makes people valuable inside an organization, and I think getting models to build it is one of the key steps toward them being genuinely useful collaborators rather than very smart new hires on their first day, every day.

r001.rationale: The response asks how models can internalize and apply new private information, but it does not ask what enables emergent generalization during pre-training or post-training.

r002.rationale: It contrasts robust learning from repeated public information with the challenge of sparse company data, then asks how to make models internalize that private information and use it for new inferences.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that got me excited about this problem is that it's really a question about continual learning, which is one of the biggest open problems in the field right now. If you think about how we use models today, they have this fixed snapshot of knowledge from pretraining, and then everything else that happens after that, we bolt on through the context window. You retrieve some documents, you paste them in, and the model reasons over them in the moment and then forgets everything.

And that works surprisingly well for a lot of things, but it's fundamentally not how a person learns. When you join a company, you don't re-read every Slack thread and design doc every morning. You absorb it. Over months you build up this internal model of how the codebase is structured, who to ask about what, why certain decisions were made. And that knowledge becomes part of how you think, not just something you look up.

So the question I find really interesting is: can we get models to do that? Can we take a company's private data, which is this long tail of stuff that's never in pretraining, and actually get it into the weights in a way that the model can use flexibly? Not just memorize the documents, but actually integrate them so it can reason with that knowledge, combine it with what it already knows, answer questions that aren't literally written down anywhere.

And it turns out that's much harder than it sounds. If you just naively fine-tune on the documents, the model will learn to regurgitate them, but it won't really generalize. There's this gap between what the data says and all the implicit things the model needs to learn from it. So a lot of what we've been thinking about is how you bridge that gap, how you turn raw data into something a model can actually learn from, and how you do that without degrading all the capabilities it already has. It touches on memory, on knowledge representation, on what it even means for a model to know something, and I think that's why it's such a rich problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses bridging the gap between document fine-tuning and generalization, but it does not ask what enables emergent generalization during pre-training or post-training.

r002.rationale: The response asks how models can absorb and flexibly use a company’s private data, but it does not ask how to make them learn it as well as familiar public knowledge or skills.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that it forces you to ask what it actually means for a model to learn something. There’s a difference between being able to retrieve a document and being able to use the knowledge in that document to make a good decision in a new situation.

And within a company, a lot of the useful knowledge isn’t neatly written down. It’s scattered across conversations, decisions, and examples of how people work. Documents disagree, things change, and some information is only relevant in a particular context. So the challenge is more than getting information into the model. It’s getting the model to understand when that information applies, what’s still current, and when it should ask someone for clarification.

That makes it a really interesting learning problem: how do you turn the experience of an organization into something a model can use and keep learning from?

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s interesting is that a company’s knowledge isn’t just a collection of facts. Some of it lives in documents, but a lot of it is implicit in how people work: why a decision was made, which exceptions matter, who you ask when something goes wrong. So getting a model to learn that knowledge forces you to ask what it actually means to understand an organization.

There’s also this interesting distinction between finding information and learning from it. A model might retrieve a document and answer a question about it, but can it use that information in a new situation? Can it recognize when something is outdated, or when two teams use the same word to mean different things? That makes it a much richer problem than just putting all your documents into a search index.
